new_entities.name: Iodine excess
new_entities.description: Iodine exposure above physiological need from diet, supplements, or iodinated contrast.

new_entities.name: Autoimmune thyroid susceptibility
new_entities.description: Risk of thyroid autoimmunity or iodine-triggered thyroid dysfunction in susceptible individuals.

edges.effect_quant: A case-control study found urinary iodine excretion above 300 µg/L was more common in hypothyroid cases than community controls (OR 0.509 for controls versus cases), and a prospective contrast cohort found abnormal TSH in 22% of adults after a single large iodine load.
edges.population: adults or pregnant women with thyroid susceptibility, prior autoimmunity risk, or sudden exposure to large iodine loads
edges.mechanism: Excess iodine can increase intrathyroidal oxidative stress, alter antigen presentation, and trigger the Wolff-Chaikoff escape problem in susceptible glands. In people with borderline thyroid reserve or autoimmune tendency, this can shift a tolerable nutrient exposure into overt dysfunction.
edges.summary: Excess iodine appears harmful in people who are susceptible to thyroid autoimmunity or thyroid dysfunction, even though the broader iodine-thyroid relationship is not simply linear. The best read is that iodine is essential but oversupply can provoke autoimmune or hypothyroid problems in vulnerable groups.
edges.caveats: This is not an argument for iodine avoidance in the general population, because deficiency is also harmful and some cohorts show a U-shaped rather than monotonic curve. The risk signal is strongest when exposure is clearly excessive or when the thyroid is already vulnerable.

evidence.notes: Does iodine excess lead to hypothyroidism? Evidence from a case-control study in India.
Urinary iodine excretion and serum thyroid function in adults after iodinated contrast administration.

effect_quant.comparator: participants developing abnormal TSH after iodinated contrast exposure

evidence.citation: Zhang X 2022 Biol Trace Elem Res
